questions.q: Which compound gives a violet colour with neutral FeCl₃ solution?
questions.explain: Phenol forms the coloured complex [Fe(OC₆H₅)₆]³⁻. Benzyl alcohol is the trap: its –OH is on an sp³ carbon, so it behaves as an alcohol and the yellow colour of FeCl₃ remains.

questions.q: Which compound also gives a coloured complex with FeCl₃, and so can be mistaken for a phenol?
questions.explain: The test really detects an –OH on an sp² carbon of a C=C (an enol unit). Ethyl acetoacetate, a β-keto ester, has a high enol content and gives a colour, while propanone exists almost entirely in the keto form and does not respond.

questions.q: Neutral ferric chloride for this test is prepared by:
options: Adding dilute NaOH dropwise to FeCl₃ solution until a slight permanent brown precipitate forms, then filtering
Boiling FeCl₃ solution with concentrated HCl
Dissolving iron filings in nitric acid
Adding excess ammonia to FeCl₃ solution and using the precipitate
questions.explain: Ordinary FeCl₃ solution is acidic because Fe³⁺ hydrolyses; neutralising it with a little NaOH and using the clear filtrate gives sharper colours. Adding acid or using the Fe(OH)₃ precipitate itself would spoil the test.

questions.q: Which phenolic compound does NOT give a characteristic colour with FeCl₃?
questions.explain: Naphthols do not give characteristic colours, so a negative FeCl₃ result does not rule out a phenol. Phenol gives violet, cresols violet or blue, and catechol a green colour that soon darkens.
